summary: How end-to-end, property and differential tests let coding agents verify their work with evidence, and what the Claude Code team does to keep its verifiers honest.
story_key: model:claude|title:how the claude code team thinks about verification
content_excerpt: How end-to-end, property and differential tests let coding agents verify their work with evidence, and what the Claude Code team does to keep its verifiers honest. On the Claude Code team, the vast majority of our code (~90%) is written and reviewed by Claude . At this scale, how we equip our agents to verify their work with evidence becomes extremely important. Verification loops are the building block that lets you delegate more work to Claude. Without them, you can really only run one or two Claudes at a time, because you have to check everything yourself. With them, you can run dozens or hundreds in parallel. That’s because giving agents a way to verify their output is an effective way to improve quality. In internal testing around structured file generation, having a separate grader check Claude’s work against a rubric improved task success by up to 10 points over a standard prompting loop, with the largest gains on the hardest problems. What was once expensive to verify (tests, benchmarks, specs, real end-to-end runs) is now cheap to request from an agent. Like code, agents can quickly generate tests, benchmarks, and specs. And once generated, these tests and benchmarks run as software so they can be run frequently without using many additional tokens. You can also close the verification loop by using the results to improve the agent’s performance on that task. For example, if an agent repeatedly fails a test that checks logs for user data, you can create a hook or a more explicit rule in your CLAUDE.md to avoid future issues. This (mostly) stops issues from happening again. So if verification is critical to producing quality code at a high velocity, what types of tests should you use and how should you apply them across your pipeline? This article answers those questions and also shares the process used by the Claude Code team. If your tests are flaky you’ll train the agent to run them again rather than fixing the failing code. If your tests are slow, the agent will do fewer tests across batches which can make pinpointing issues difficult. Heavier tests are best deployed before you’ve committed the changes. If you have to focus on one test type, pick end-to-end. These tests describe real user flows like adding an item to a cart, checking out, and moving to a confirmation page. This is output from the reference server . Much of the work done with a developer product is now done by someone's AI agent. When the agent hits a bug, a wrong result or a tool that can't do what was asked, it works around the problem or gives up. The developer may never hear about it, and the company behind the product might not know that anything is wrong. Many MCP servers gained a feedback tool during 2026, each under a different name and almost all one-way: the report goes in and nothing comes back. Support tools still assume a person typing into a chat window. It is written with developer tools in mind, where an AI coding agent builds an integration with your product. content_excerpt: Kubernetes’ next AI push targets GPU efficiency, massive clusters, and safer agents. SALT LAKE CITY — I’m often surprised how many people don’t know just how important Kubernetes is to AI. After all, in the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) January 2026 Annual Cloud Native Survey , 66% of organizations hosting generative AI models use Kubernetes for their inference workloads. Throw in everyone who runs other kinds of AI workloads on Kubernetes, and it’s clear a majority of AI users depend on Kubernetes for their workloads. So, at KubeCon North America 2026 , both the CNCF and vendors presented the next wave of Kubernetes improvements, designed to keep AI productive while making the most of their cloud infrastructure with smarter scheduling, larger control planes, faster container startup, and tighter controls over autonomous agents. Kubernetes 1.38 , scheduled for December 16, is the next milestone. So you can expect, as an early Christmas present, gang scheduling and additional accelerator-allocation capabilities advancing toward stable status. But the conference’s message extended beyond one release. Other important improvements are also arriving through Karpenter. This open-source, high-performance Kubernetes node lifecycle manager automatically provisions and terminates compute resources in response to unscheduled pod requests and other emerging CNCF projects. As Mike Stefaniak, AWS’s Head of Containers, said in his keynote, “AI workloads can spin up 10s of 1000s of GPU instances per cluster, and things break at that scale.” To address this, fixes discovered in enormous production deployments should go upstream rather than remain inside a provider’s private fork. title: Show HN: We submitted 105 AI-built contact forms – 27 said "sent", sent nothing

content_excerpt: Do contact forms on AI-built sites send anything? A Playwright harness that checks without sending, with known-answer fixtures and the study's method and results. We submitted the contact form on public Lovable and Bolt sites while recording every network request and blocking all of them , so no message ever reached a site owner. On the final run, 27 of 105 forms showed a success message ("Message sent!") and sent nothing; 54 of 105 sent the typed message. On sites without demo signs, 16 of 73 were fake. After the contact form is found, every request is intercepted. Same-origin static files and cross-origin scripts, styles and fonts load; everything else is recorded and aborted . The harness fills visible fields with obvious test values (never honeypots), presses send and watches the page for five seconds. Open DevTools → Network and press send: a working form adds a request that carries the text you typed. The write-up's fix section lists three ways to fix it. Coding agents (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex) can install a skill that adds a working form and replaces fake handlers: Nothing is submitted to anyone. title: From tasks to goals
summary: LangChain CEO and Co-founder Harrison Chase shares how we're moving from task-specific agents to goal-focused agents. Learn more.
story_key: story|title:from tasks to goals
content_excerpt: As agents become more powerful, we’re moving from giving them tasks to giving them goals. Under the hood, this move from tasks to goals consists of two more practical shifts: This is changes what an agent does, what it needs, how its built, and we interact with it. Previously, the user would specify tasks. Now, the user specifies a goal, and the agent iterates towards that goal by deconstructing into tasks, doing some of them, updating the task list, etc. The agent needs to be good at brainstorming and selecting different tasks, which requires new context engineering and prompting strategies. It needs to be somewhat creative - and varied - in brainstorming potential tasks (if it keeps on suggesting the same tasks over and over again, that’s not great). Practical consideration: you need some way to see what tasks the agent is doing (e.g. a to-do list), as well as prompting for the agent to be creative in coming up with tasks When you give an agent task, you largely have an idea of what tools it will call. When you give it a goal - you don’t really know what tools it will call, and you may not even know what tools it will need to call. Practical consideration: you need more controls over what tools an agent can or cannot call When you give an agent a task, you’re naturally in the loop. If you don’t provide all the information up front, its easy for the agent to ask follow up questions in chat. When you give an agent a goal - it may be running in the background and need to get clarification on certain points. It needs a way to ask questions to humans - whether through Slack or a dedicated UI. Practical consideration: you need a mechanism for a background agent to ask you for clarification The agent needs to know how its doing as it progresses towards a goal. This could either be by checking in on a metric to see if it is improving, or by getting explicit feedback from a human on how its doing. The more closely tied to a metric, the better in some sense (easy for it to track automatically!) but its never wise to blindly optimize a metric, so explicit human feedback may be the best thing. This is why its important to design goals in a way where its easy to give feedback. You can have both metrics for the agent to drive towards, and a way to get feedback from users. content_excerpt: Author a Feature once, serve it everywhere — one declarative definition powers point-in-time training and warm online ranking at p95 34 ms, with in-session signals live in under 130 ms. Real-time personalization depends on understanding what customers want in the moment. When a retail banking customer checks their accounts, explores credit cards, or opens a loan calculator, each interaction signals their current intent. A relevant offer needs to reach them while they're still in the session. The challenge is making that intent available to the model. Raw clickstream data must be aggregated into time-windowed features for two purposes: training on historical values as they existed at a given point in time, and serving predictions using current values with millisecond latency. Building these pipelines separately creates duplicate feature definitions that can drift over time and degrade model accuracy. Databricks Feature Views solve this by letting you define features once for both training and serving. In this blog, we'll walk through an open-source Solution Accelerator that uses Feature Views to build a real-time next-best-offer (NBO) recommender for financial services. The accelerator includes two parts: a recommender using batch features and an extension that adds streaming, in-session intent. Both are built end-to-end on Databricks, with runnable notebooks you can clone and deploy. Real-time recommendations require both consistency and speed. Features must be computed the same way during training and serving to avoid train/serve skew, which can degrade model accuracy. At inference time, those features must also be retrieved and scored in milliseconds. Traditionally, meeting both requirements meant maintaining separate systems: a batch pipeline for training features and a hand-written streaming job for online serving. This creates duplicate logic that can drift over time. Feature Views eliminate the need for separate feature definitions. You declare the logic once, and Databricks reuses it across training and serving: At training time, the create_training_set API retrieves feature values as they existed at each labeled event, preventing future data leakage. At inference time, the Model Serving endpoint fetches batch features from the online store using customer_id . title: Why we rebuilt LangSmith around the agent
summary: We reorganized LangSmith around a single agent record. Build, run, improve, and govern every agent from one place, on any framework or runtime.
story_key: story|title:why we rebuilt langsmith around the agent
content_excerpt: Last week we announced our series C and introduced the new LangSmith Agent Platform : a single place to build, run, improve, and govern every agent. With this, agents are now the core object across LangSmith, connecting fragmented workflows for developers and enabling platform teams to manage agents across the business. In this post, we discuss why we reorganized the product, how the agent model works, what it unlocks, and where we're taking it next. 2026 brought a step change in agent adoption as new harnesses , models, and engineering approaches made it possible to build agents that can reliably perform complex, high value work . Companies now run many agents across the business: engineering uses coding agents, product is building customer-facing agents, and teams across the organization have various internal productivity agents. These agents are built with different frameworks, hosted on various runtimes, and use a variety of tools and models. Engineers work across disconnected surfaces. Tracing , monitoring , and deployments all live in different places. This requires frequent context switching, and in practice results in teams skipping difficult but important steps like building the evals. AI Platform teams have difficulty answering basic governance questions. Which agents exist, and who owns each of them? What do they cost, and how are they performing? When costs spike, there is often no obvious person to ask what happened. We wanted to make it simple for teams to manage the entire agent development lifecycle from one place, using any stack, with ownership and governance across all of it. LangSmith supports the entire agent development lifecycle: build, run, improve, and govern. Now, we've connected the entire process through a unique agent record. When you open an agent record, its traces, evals, Agent Server, and Engine issues are accessible with one click, so you don’t need to navigate multiple surfaces to find them. Each agent’s local, dev, staging, and production environments sit under the same agent ID, so comparing performance after making changes is simple. LangSmith is composable, so you can choose the parts you need. If you already run your agent on another platform, you can connect it to LangSmith to improve and govern it without changing any other workflows. title: Can KV Cache Be Reused Across Model Updates? A DeepSeek-V4-Flash Case Study
summary: Reusing key--value (KV) caches across language model updates could avoid repeated computation of shared context, but changes in model weights raise a fundamental question about what these caches preserve. We investigate direct cache reuse across four model updates, with a detailed study of DeepSeek-V4-Flash to Flash-0731. Our central finding is that caches can retain useful task information without faithfully reproducing the updated model's behavior. Retrieval accuracy varies substantially across updates, ranging from near-native performance to large losses. With source caches already available, reuse achieves median time-to-first-token speedups of $2.10$--$5.08\times$ on three longer-prefix QA benchmarks. To characterize the behavioral differences behind these outcomes, we introduce Functional Cache Divergence, which compares next-token distributions under reused and native caches. Direct KV cache reuse better preserves native model behavior in natural-text continuation, whereas compatibility degrades with increasing prefix length in single-token retrieval tasks. Answer-margin analyses help explain how correct retrieval decisions survive substantial internal state changes. Yet even agreement on the first generated token does not ensure agreement in answer content or stopping behavior. These findings establish task utility and fidelity to native inference as distinct criteria for evaluating cross-version KV cache reuse.

title: From Bytes to Behavior: Request-Level Attribution from Live GPU Hidden States
summary: Existing memory forensics for machine learning systems typically targets static artifacts, such as model weights or prompt logs, rather than the transient computational states of a live inference process. This gap limits an examiner's ability to analyze the specific behavior of a running large language model (LLM) service that cannot be restarted or modified. We present a method for acquiring per-layer residual-stream activations from a live GPU process using a non-modifying debugger, without requiring prior knowledge of the model's architecture parameters or weights. The approach employs a general six-stage process with platform-specific adapters, utilizing either a PyTorch allocator clock or a kernel-launch clock to identify and read tensor allocations from video memory. We validate this acquisition on 33 open-source decoder-only models across nine architecture classes, demonstrating that the recovered bytes are byte-exact and usable for downstream analysis. As a use case, we apply linear probes trained on standard framework activations to the recovered states, successfully distinguishing refusal from compliance with an AUROC of 0.88 on held-out prompts. This work establishes that live, observational access to intermediate hidden states is feasible on named inference platforms, providing a new source of evidence for examining the operational behavior of deployed AI systems.

title: New AI agent observability and governance across BigQuery and Looker
summary:
As enterprises move AI agents from experimental prototypes into production, data and platform teams are discovering that deploying an agent is only half the battle — you also need to see how it reasons, which data it touches, and what it costs to run. Today, we are announcing expanded AI agent observability and evaluation capabilities across Google Data Cloud, giving you unified visibility into your first-party (1P) data agents in BigQuery and Looker as well as custom third-party (3P) agents built with agent development frameworks such as Agent Development Kit (ADK) or LangGraph.

Putting conversational and autonomous agents into production requires solving three operational challenges: tracing multi-step reasoning while protecting sensitive data, controlling token consumption and query spend, and evaluating answer accuracy before prompt or schema changes reach users. Let’s explore how our new agent observability and evaluation capabilities help you do this. 

What's new: Agent observability across Data Cloud

Running agents at scale means you need to see how they perform, what they cost, and what actions they take. We're rolling out a unified telemetry framework across Google's Agentic Data Cloud that works the same way for every agent: Capture telemetry from the agent, land it in BigQuery tables you own, and analyze it wherever your teams already work.

1. Capture telemetry from every first-party and custom agent

  • First-party data agents: Out-of-the-box Conversational Analytics agents emit telemetry automatically with no setup required. Queries routed to BigQuery data agents in Gemini Enterprise through agent-to-agent (A2A) workflows (now GA) send Cloud Monitoring metrics, Cloud Trace spans, and BigQuery conversation logs straight into your agent's project.

  • Custom agents: Agents built with ADK or LangGraph stream the same structured telemetry into BigQuery through single-line SDK instrumentation.

2. Land telemetry in one governed home in BigQuery

  • Conversation logging in BigQuery (GA): Managed 1P conversation logging writes to BigQuery tables you own, so you can inspect Conversational Analytics traces, including prompts and responses, directly in your data warehouse.

  • Governed by default: The Conversational Analytics API, now GA, includes always-on admin audit logs and optional data-read audit logs in Cloud Audit Logs, and supports VPC Service Controls, customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK), and regional and multi-regional data residency.

3. Analyze with dashboards wherever your teams work

  • In BigQuery (GA): Agent monitoring provides prebuilt dashboards in BigQuery Studio to track usage, active sessions, top knowledge sources, and latency across BigQuery Conversational Analytics agents.

  • In Looker (GA): System Activity dashboards for Conversational Analytics, now GA in Looker (Google Cloud core) and Looker (original), track engagement and token usage, while user ratings and query review in the Responses & feedback tab are in preview.
  • Build your own: Create interactive reports with the open-source Data Studio template or deploy the ready-made Looker Block for Agent Analytics for real-time custom agent monitoring.

Tracing agent reasoning and protecting privacy

Enterprise observability requires balancing diagnostic telemetry with strict data privacy boundaries. Because tracking features involve ingestion and storage costs, Google Data Cloud separates operational telemetry from conversation content so admins and agent owners can govern each layer independently.

At the project or organization level, admins can enable Cloud Monitoring (aggregate metrics such as request volume, latency, and token usage) and Cloud Trace (step-by-step spans for each request) across their environment, using Cloud Trace observability scopes to consolidate telemetry across multiple agent projects. To protect sensitive data, these operational metrics and sanitized first-party trace spans exclude customer core content (such as user prompts, model responses, internal thoughts, and generated SQL).

When you need deeper transcript auditing, agent owners and editors can opt in to conversation logging on a per-agent basis:

  • Governed conversation logging in BigQuery: When enabled, a Google-managed service agent streams user prompts, responses, and turn-level telemetry into a customer-owned BigQuery table (agent_events) via the BigQuery Storage Write API, inheriting your dataset's IAM permissions, CMEK, and VPC Service Controls. Built-in privacy guardrails enforce a fail-closed check before each turn — skipping logging whenever a knowledge source uses row-level security, column-level policy tags, or dynamic data masking — while fail-open execution keeps your users' chat sessions uninterrupted if a logging error occurs.

  • Full trace trees for custom 3P agents: While 1P conversation logging intentionally strips low-level tool arguments and internal SQL, developers building custom agents on ADK or LangGraph can instrument their code with the open-source ADK plugin (BigQueryAgentAnalyticsPlugin). With a single-line setup, the SDK streams full tool-invocation execution trees, time-series telemetry, and multimodal payloads straight into BigQuery.

  • In-warehouse root cause and drift analysis: Because conversation logs land natively in your agent_events table, you don't need separate export pipelines to diagnose failures. You can run BigQuery AI functions (such as AI.GENERATE to summarize error patterns and AI.EMBED with VECTOR_SEARCH to cluster recurring issues) or use the open-source bigquery-agent-analytics Python SDK and Colab starter notebook for post-hoc semantic drift clustering and LLM-as-a-judge sentiment analysis.

Controlling token costs with FinOps guardrails

As agent adoption grows, FinOps and platform teams need clear visibility into consumption alongside active controls to prevent runaway spend. With promotional trial pricing currently available for Conversational Analytics, now is a good time to establish baseline usage and cost guardrails:

  • Granular token and latency tracking: In BigQuery conversation logs, each turn records input, output, thought, cached, and total token counts alongside total turn latency, while Looker System Activity reports estimated input and output tokens across your business intelligence (BI) workloads.

  • Turnkey observability dashboards: You can track projected token usage and engagement in the BigQuery Studio Monitoring tab and native Looker System Activity dashboards, or query agent_events log data via BigQuery SQL using the open-source seven-page Data Studio report template and self-hosted Streamlit app in the BigQuery Agent Analytics GitHub repository.

  • Active query and token spend caps: To prevent unexpected charges before they happen, you can configure per-query BigQuery byte scan caps (big_query_max_billed_bytes) on your agent, which use dry-run estimates to block oversized queries without incurring on-demand scan charges. For BigQuery and the Conversational Analytics API, you can also enforce daily input and output token quotas (in preview) per project, user, or agent in the Google Cloud console and gcloud CLI.

Evaluating and benchmarking your AI agents

Runtime observability works alongside systematic evaluation. While logs and traces tell you how an agent behaved in production, evaluation benchmarks verify whether updates to your prompts, models, or data schemas improve SQL accuracy and answer quality before users experience a regression:

  • Benchmarking with Prism: Our open-source evaluation tool, Prism, lets you test Conversational Analytics agents grounded in BigQuery tables or Looker Explores via the Conversational Analytics API using reusable test suites, regex assertions, and multi-region agent discovery (deployed behind an access layer such as Cloud IAP).

  • Unified evaluation and production analytics: Prism can stream completed evaluation runs directly into day-partitioned BigQuery tables in your project, placing your pre-deployment benchmark scores right alongside your production agent_events logs for side-by-side analysis in BigQuery and Looker.

  • Native BigQuery evaluations: First-party agent evaluations in BigQuery (built on the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform evaluation service with bring-your-own-service-account support) are available in preview via API and a guided Colab notebook.

Getting started

Ready to bring visibility, governance, and cost control to your AI agents? Here is how to get started in three steps:

  1. Enable first-party agent observability. Turn on Cloud Monitoring and Cloud Trace in your project and opt in to per-agent conversation logging using the BigQuery agent monitoring guide, and track BI token consumption with the Looker Conversational Analytics overview and Looker System Activity documentation.

  2. Instrument custom agents and deploy analytics dashboards. Add the BigQuery Agent Analytics SDK to your ADK or LangGraph agents, launch the open-source Data Studio report template or Streamlit app, and explore in-warehouse log analysis with the Colab starter notebook.

  3. Benchmark your agents and set cost guardrails. Run automated accuracy suites with Prism, and configure BigQuery byte scan caps and daily token quotas via Manage BigQuery costs for agents.

title: Release 2.74.0 corresponding to NGC container 26.10
summary:
Triton Inference Server

The Triton Inference Server provides a cloud inferencing solution optimized for both CPUs and GPUs. The server provides an inference service via an HTTP or GRPC endpoint, allowing remote clients to request inferencing for any model being managed by the server. For edge deployments, Triton Server is also available as a shared library with an API that allows the full functionality of the server to be included directly in an application.

New Features and Improvements

  • The S3 addressing style is now configurable.
  • Request cancellation is now checked before a request is dispatched to the backend, and before batch assembly in the TensorRT backend.
  • Tutorials: The Llava1.5 guide is deprecated in favor of the new Qwen2.5-VL guide for the TensorRT-LLM PyTorch backend. Note: this is a breaking change.
  • HTTP request buffers are now released after a request is rejected for exceeding the chunk limit.
  • --http-max-input-size is now enforced across nested parameters of generate requests.
  • SageMaker model URLs are now validated before path normalization.
  • Fixed copying of the cuBLAS libraries to the CUDA targets lib directory.
  • Relaxed the openai and pydantic pins to match vLLM requirements.
  • Tritonserver is now built on, and shipped on, the cuda-dl-base devel image.
  • Python backend: Restrictive permissions are now applied to shared memory, and GPU tensor allocation now falls back to host memory.
  • ONNX Runtime, OpenVINO, Python and TensorRT-LLM backends: Backend builds now require TRITON_BUILD_CONTAINER instead of synthesizing a py3-min image.
  • vLLM backend: Added support for vLLM >= 0.30, and prompts are now rendered before generation and encoding.
  • Triton CLI: The image fetch in the TRT-LLM preprocessing template is now bounded.

Known Issues

  • The Triton TensorRT-LLM Backend container image is not included in this release.
  • vLLM's v0 API and Ray are affected by vulnerabilities. Users should consider their own architecture and mitigation steps which may include but should not be limited to:
    • Do not expose Ray executors and vLLM hosts to a network where any untrusted connections might reach the host.
    • Ensure that only the other vLLM hosts are able to connect to the TCP port used for the XPUB socket. Note that the port used is random.
  • When using Valgrind or other leak detection tools on AGX-Thor or DGX-Spark systems, you might see memory leaks attributed to NvRmGpuLibOpen.
  • Valgrind or other memory leak detection tools may occasionally report leaks related to DCGM. These reports are intermittent and often disappear on retry.
  • CuPy has issues with the CUDA 13 Device API in multithreaded contexts. Avoid using tritonclient cuda_shared_memory APIs in multithreaded environments until fixed by CuPy.
  • TensorRT calibration cache may require size adjustment in some cases, which was observed for the IGX platform.
  • The core Python binding may incur an additional D2H and H2D copy if the backend and frontend both specify device memory to be used for response tensors.
  • A segmentation fault related to DCGM and NSCQ may be encountered during server shutdown on NVSwitch systems. A possible workaround for this issue is to disable the collection of GPU metrics tritonserver --allow-gpu-metrics false ....
  • When using TensorRT models, if auto-complete configuration is disabled and is_non_linear_format_io:true for reformat-free tensors is not provided in the model configuration, the model may not load successfully.
  • When using Python models in decoupled mode, users need to ensure that the ResponseSender goes out of scope or is properly cleaned up before unloading the model to guarantee that the unloading process executes correctly.
  • Triton Inference Server with vLLM backend currently does not support running vLLM models with tensor parallelism sizes greater than 1 and the default "distributed_executor_backend" setting when using explicit model control mode. In attempt to load a vllm model (tp > 1) in explicit mode, users could potentially see failure at initialize step: could not acquire lock for <_io.BufferedWriter name='<stdout>'> at interpreter shutdown, possibly due to daemon threads. For the default model control mode, after server shutdown, vllm related sub-processes are not killed. Related vllm issue: vllm-project/vllm#6766. Please specify "distributed_executor_backend":"ray" in the model.json when deploying vllm models with tensor parallelism > 1.
  • When loading models with file override, multiple model configuration files are not supported. Users must provide the model configuration by setting parameter "config" : "<JSON>" instead of custom configuration file in the following format: "file:configs/<model-config-name>.pbtxt" : "<base64-encoded-file-content>".
  • TensorRT-LLM backend provides limited support of Triton extensions and features.
  • The TensorRT-LLM backend may core dump on server shutdown. This impacts server teardown only and will not impact inferencing.
  • The Java CAPI is known to have intermittent segfaults.
  • Some systems which implement malloc() may not release memory back to the operating system right away causing a false memory leak. This can be mitigated by using a different malloc implementation. Tcmalloc and jemalloc are installed in the Triton container and can be used by specifying the library in LD_PRELOAD. NVIDIA recommends experimenting with both tcmalloc and jemalloc to determine which one works better for your use case.
  • Auto-complete may cause an increase in server start time. To avoid a start time increase, users can provide the full model configuration and launch the server with --disable-auto-complete-config.
  • Auto-complete does not support PyTorch models due to lack of metadata in the model. It can only verify that the number of inputs and the input names matches what is specified in the model configuration. There is no model metadata about the number of outputs and datatypes. Related PyTorch bug: pytorch/pytorch#38273
  • Triton Client PIP wheels for ARM SBSA are not available from PyPI and pip will install an incorrect Jetson version of Triton Client library for Arm SBSA. The correct client wheel file can be pulled directly from the Arm SBSA SDK image and manually installed.
  • Traced models in PyTorch seem to create overflows when int8 tensor values are transformed to int32 on the GPU. Refer to pytorch/pytorch#66930 for more information.
  • Triton cannot retrieve GPU metrics with MIG-enabled GPU devices.
  • Triton metrics might not work if the host machine is running a separate DCGM agent on bare-metal or in a container.

Client Libraries and Examples

The client libraries and examples are available in this release exclusively via the Ubuntu 24.04–based NGC Container. The SDK container includes the client libraries and examples, Performance Analyzer, and Model Analyzer. See Getting the Client Libraries for more information.

ManyLinux Assets (early access)

This release was compiled with AlmaLinux 8.9 based out of manylinux_2_34 and can be used on RHEL 9 and later versions.
See the included README.md for complete details about installation, verification, and support.
This release supports ensembles. Confirm CUDA, TensorRT, ONNX Runtime, PyTorch, and Python versions in the shipped README.md.
Some optional backend features such as the PyTorch backend's TorchTRT extension are not currently supported.
